newsitem.title: UK: Courtaulds says some improvement in viscose.
newsitem.headline: Courtaulds says some improvement in viscose.

text.p: Courtaulds Plc, which is the biggest producer of viscose rayon in Europe and North America, said on Wednesday that there were signs of recovery in the depressed viscose market, but that the recovery was so far not significant.

In an interview with Reuters, chief executive Gordon Campbell said massive destocking of viscose had come to an end and the market had seen a producer price rise in January after a long run of price falls.
Courtauld's largest competitor in viscose, Austria's Lenzing AG, announced a further price rise last month.

"Assuming that that second price hike sticks...by the end of June there will have been a 10-percent price hike in viscose in Europe, which is indicative of a recovery in the market. So in that respect there is some improvement, but it is from such a lousy base that I'm not really celebrating," Campbell said.
The viscose market has been hit by a huge increase in production capacity, particularly in the Far East, and by changes in fashion. The material is used principally for printed clothing.
"There has been too much capacity in my view put in in Asia in an attempt to chase a market that isn't there," Campbell said.

Last month Courtaulds cut its European production capacity for viscose by 20 percent in response to the weak market conditions, shifting manpower to a forthcoming British plant for Tencel, where demand is well ahead of supply.
Campbell said further cuts in capacity were possible, depending on the strength of the recovery in the viscose market.
Courtauld's aim is to reduce the proportion of acrylic and viscose fibres in its overall sales through growth in its coatings and plastic packaging businesses, as well as in Tencel, Campbell said.
But he added that selling the viscose operation was not a realistic option.

"We are better at running the viscose business than anybody else, and the same is true of acrylics, so it is likely to be worth more to us than to anyone else. And it is extremely unlikely there is a purchaser out there," he said.
Although the viscose and acrylic operations were not likely to grow, he said both were still capable of strong cash generation as the cycle turned up.

"If I thought there was a purchaser out there who would pay fair value I would certainly consider whether we wanted to keep them, but as there isn't the only thing we can do is run them as effectively as we can and extract as much cash from them as we can," he added.
